title: From Daguerreotypes to Deep Space: 175 Years of Solar Eclipse Photography
excerpt: As today's total eclipse sweeps across Greenland, Iceland, and Spain, a look at the images that changed astronomy — from an 1851 silver plate to NASA's hour-long eclipse from lunar orbit.
body:
• Today marks the 2026 total solar eclipse, visible across Greenland, Iceland, and Spain — the first total eclipse since April 2024 and the last until 2027.
  • Eclipse photography spans 175 years, from Johann Berkowski's pioneering 1851 daguerreotype to NASA's Artemis II crew capturing an hour-long eclipse from lunar orbit in April 2026.
  • Arthur Eddington's 1919 eclipse photographs from the island of Principe provided the first evidence for Einstein's theory of general relativity.
  • The European Space Agency's Proba-3 mission now creates artificial eclipses lasting hours using a two-satellite formation, producing over 50 last year alone.

On this day — August 12, 2026 — a total solar eclipse sweeps across Greenland, Iceland, and Spain, plunging a narrow corridor of Earth into midday darkness. For the millions in the path of totality, the experience will last only minutes. But our record of these celestial events stretches back millennia, and the photographs born from that obsession have fundamentally changed how we understand the sun.

The Image That Started It All

The first photograph of a total solar eclipse clear enough to be scientifically useful was taken exactly 175 years ago today. On July 28, 1851, Johann Julius Friedrich Berkowski set up at the Royal Observatory in Königsberg, Prussia (now Kaliningrad, Russia), attached a small telescope to a heliometer, and exposed a daguerreotype plate for 84 seconds as the moon crossed the sun.

The result was remarkable: not only was the corona visible, but several eruptions could be seen blasting from the sun's edges over the moon's silhouette. "Solar astronomy would never be the same," wrote science historian William B. Ashworth Jr. Yet Berkowski himself remained so obscure that his full name wasn't confirmed until a 2013 German article.

After Berkowski, eclipse photography spread rapidly. William and Frederick Langenheim captured miniature daguerreotypes in Philadelphia in 1854. By the late 19th century, expeditions to photograph eclipses had become major scientific undertakings.

The Eclipse That Proved Einstein Right

No eclipse photograph has had greater scientific impact than those taken on May 29, 1919, by British astronomer Arthur Eddington on the island of Principe off the west coast of Africa. Eddington's team photographed stars positioned close to the sun during totality and compared their apparent positions to where they appeared when the sun was elsewhere in the sky.

The comparison confirmed that the sun's gravity bent starlight exactly as Albert Einstein's general theory of relativity predicted. The finding, announced later that year, made Einstein a global celebrity and reshaped our understanding of gravity, space, and time.

From Film to Digital: The Modern Revolution

The leap from glass plates to digital sensors transformed eclipse science. Astronomer Shadia Habbal at the University of Hawaii, who has chased eclipses since the mid-1990s, told Smithsonian Magazine that modern cameras offer an immediate advantage: "You can more or less see your data right away after the eclipse, and you can work with it more easily."

"The science is so compelling, because each image, each new eclipse, gives us new ideas."

— Shadia Habbal, University of Hawaii Institute for Astronomy

Today's composite images — some stitching together thousands of individual photographs — reveal the sun's corona in stunning detail, exposing the wispy magnetic structures that drive space weather and can disrupt satellites, power grids, and communications on Earth.

Andrew McCarthy, a prominent astrophotographer, traveled to Missouri during the April 2024 eclipse and combined data from five cameras compositing thousands of photos during the four minutes of totality to produce what became one of the most widely shared eclipse images in history.

Eclipses From Space: Artemis II and Proba-3

The most extraordinary eclipse photographs of 2026 were captured before today's event. In April, NASA's Artemis II crew aboard the Orion spacecraft photographed a total solar eclipse from lunar orbit — watching the sun hide behind the moon for nearly an hour, far longer than any eclipse visible from Earth.

Because the astronauts were so close to the moon, it appeared much larger than the sun, and the transit took far longer than the minutes-long events on Earth's surface. The resulting images show the sun's corona streaming outward in filaments, with the jagged lunar horizon revealing backlit mountain topography.

Meanwhile, the European Space Agency's Proba-3 mission, launched in December 2024, has pioneered artificial eclipses using two satellites flying in precise formation 492 feet apart. One satellite blocks the sun's light from the other's coronagraph. Last year, the mission produced more than 50 artificial eclipses, with the longest lasting about five and a half hours.

"The natural one is still better quality, because the moon is so far and it covers a little bit less than what we cover with Proba-3."

— Andrei Zhukov, Royal Observatory of Belgium

Today's Eclipse and What's Ahead

Today's path of totality crosses Greenland, Iceland, and northern Spain, including the Balearic Islands and central Spain. NASA's eclipse program manager Kelly Korreck has noted that humans have been documenting eclipses since roughly 3000 B.C. — a Pueblo rock carving discovered in New Mexico in 1992 may depict a total eclipse from July 11, 1097.

For those who miss today's event, the wait won't be long. Next year's total eclipse, visible from parts of North Africa and the Middle East, will be the longest of the century at close to six minutes of totality.

As Smithsonian visualization scientist Kimberly Arcand puts it: "Images can tell stories across generations. We are able to create moments that last beyond that just very ephemeral, little, tiny piece of time."
